This suggests (i) higher-than-normal walking speed, (ii) outward dispersal rather than convergence, (iii) stronger directional organization (not random headings), (iv) paths that remain fairly linear while rerouting, (v) reduced lingering, (vi) spatial re-allocation away from one lane (more spread / less concentration), and (vii) a clear temporal trend: dispersal/spread increasing over time as the lane clears. Trend metrics are only used where the description explicitly implies change (“clear the affected lane”). Expected bands are chosen to overlap real pedestrian ranges while excluding at least one trivial baseline (RANDOM or STOP) per question.

questions.question: V — Are pedestrians moving at purposeful escape speeds (brisk but not running) rather than stopping or jittering randomly?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: “Escaping / heading far away” implies brisk walking and possibly brief rushing, aligning with real-data rushing/running (1.5–2.5) and above normal transit (0.8–1.3). The band excludes RANDOM mean_speed (~3.96–3.99) and STOP (0.0).

An escape response typically includes some heterogeneity (accelerations/decelerations while clearing the lane), fitting mixed transit/festival CV (0.40–0.80) and possibly as low as homogeneous flow (0.3–0.5). This metric alone overlaps RANDOM (~0.58), but bundled with mean_speed it becomes discriminative (RANDOM fails mean_speed; STOP fails both).

questions.question: T — Is there a clear temporal increase in spreading out as the sprinkler lane gets cleared?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: “People clear the affected lane” implies the crowd expands away from the sprinkler area over time, matching the real-data ‘expanding’ spread_trend (0.10–0.40). This excludes RANDOM/STOP near 0.

As agents leave a constrained lane for open sections, local neighbor counts should reduce (dispersing), aligning with real-data ‘clearly dispersing’ density_trend (-0.40 to -0.10). Using max -0.1 avoids the near-zero band that overlaps RANDOM/STOP.

questions.question: D — Do pedestrians exhibit organized escape directions (not isotropic/random headings) while moving toward drier areas?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Heading for “drier open sections far away” implies a dominant set of directions (organized avoidance), consistent with mostly-directional real scenes (0.55–0.75) and below mixed transit (0.75–0.90). Setting max 0.8 excludes RANDOM (=1.0).
Lane-clearing toward a shared dry region should produce moderate-to-high alignment (typical transit 0.30–0.55 up to festival/event flow 0.55–0.85). This excludes RANDOM (0.05–0.15) and STOP (0.0).

questions.question: S — Do pedestrians relocate into broader open areas (less spatial concentration than a single-lane occupancy) after sprinkler activation?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Moving from an affected lane into “open sections” suggests occupancy becomes less like a single tight cluster (>0.55) and more like a transit-like spread (0.25–0.55). This also avoids STOP’s typical ~0.41 only by itself; bundling with dispersal_score below ensures STOP is excluded.

“Clear the affected lane” implies outward motion away from an initial crowded lane region, matching explicit dispersal/flee real-data (0.30–0.80) while allowing slightly lower due to partial/scene-specific geometry. This excludes RANDOM (dispersal_score negative) and STOP (0.0).

questions.question: R — Are trajectories plausibly pedestrian-like (mostly straight segments toward a destination) rather than random-walk zigzags or frozen positions?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Heading “far away” toward dry sections implies purposeful, near-straight paths with mild detours around obstacles, consistent with real pedestrian transit (0.85–0.97). This excludes RANDOM (~0.02) and STOP (0.0).

questions.question: T/V — Do pedestrians accelerate into motion to clear the sprinkler-affected area (mobilization rather than halting)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: A sprinkler activation implies a behavioral change toward faster movement; a positive normalized slope corresponds to real-data ‘clearly accelerating’ (0.10–0.40). This excludes RANDOM/STOP near 0.

As the crowd mobilizes to clear the lane, the fraction of slow/lingering agents should decrease over time (mobilizing: -0.40 to -0.10). Using max -0.1 avoids the trivial near-0 trend band that overlaps RANDOM/STOP.

questions.question: S/R — Do pedestrians avoid remaining stationary in the sprinkler zone (low lingering overall) while still exhibiting realistic motion (not random)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Escaping/clearing behavior implies few agents have mean speed below 0.3 m/s, closer to active transit (0.00–0.10) and below viewing/queueing. Setting max 0.15 excludes STOP (1.0). (RANDOM also has 0.0, so we bundle with alignment to exclude RANDOM.)
Organized motion toward dry sections should yield at least transit-level alignment (>0.30), and requiring min 0.4 excludes RANDOM (0.05–0.15) and STOP (0.0).

scenes.description: A trivia game along the promenade encourages teams to move between clues and submit answers at stations.
scenes.decomposition_reasoning: A participatory trivia game implies mixed stop-and-go motion (teams walking between clue stations and lingering to submit answers), generally purposeful trajectories along a promenade (high path linearity, non-random direction distribution), moderate crowd self-organization (some common travel directions but not a single-file stream), and non-panic interpersonal spacing (near-zero physical contacts). The questions cover velocity, realism/path quality, direction/flow, spatial distribution, temporal stop-go patterning, and crowd interaction/safety. Trend metrics are used only for the explicitly implied stop-and-go temporal changes, and bands are chosen to exclude at least one trivial baseline (RANDOM or STOP) per question.

questions.question: V: Do participants move at normal walking speeds (not frozen, not random-jitter fast), consistent with walking between trivia stations?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Walking between stations suggests normal urban transit rather than rushing: real-data mean_speed is ~0.8-1.3 (urban transit) and can dip toward ~0.4-0.9 in congested/pause-heavy scenes; using 0.5-1.3 allows stop-and-go while excluding RANDOM (~3.96) and excluding pure STOP (0).

Stop-and-go between clues plus brief lingering at stations implies mixed speeds; real mixed transit/festival CV is ~0.40-0.80 (Lyon median ~0.52). Pairing with mean_speed makes this informative despite RANDOM overlap (random CV ~0.58). This band also excludes STOP (0).

questions.question: R: Are trajectories purposeful and route-like along the promenade (not erratic random walks), consistent with moving between successive clue stations?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Between-station travel is typically near-straight over camera windows; real pedestrian transit is ~0.85-0.97. Using 0.82-0.97 allows minor detours around obstacles/people while strongly excluding RANDOM (path_linearity ~0.02) and excluding STOP (0).

A promenade with stations yields non-uniform heading choices (some dominant directions along the walkway), so entropy should be below near-uniform random. Real mixed transit is ~0.75-0.90; setting max 0.90 excludes RANDOM (=1.0). (STOP is 0, which is allowed; the bundle already excludes STOP via path_linearity/min>0.82.)

questions.question: D: Is there moderate-to-strong directional organization (people largely moving along the promenade between stations) rather than chaotic headings?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Promenade travel tends to align velocities along the corridor; with teams moving both ways, alignment should be above typical chaotic (0.10-0.30) but not near-uniform stream (0.80+). Real urban transit is ~0.30-0.55; event-like flows can reach 0.55-0.85. The band min 0.35 excludes RANDOM (<0.22) and excludes STOP (0).

Two-way/multi-station travel implies 'mostly directional' to 'mixed transit' entropy (0.55-0.90) but not uniform random (1.0). Setting max 0.88 helps exclude RANDOM; min 0.6 avoids a degenerate near-single-direction case. (STOP at 0 is excluded by min 0.6.)

questions.question: S: Do people distribute across multiple clue/answer stations rather than forming a single dominant cluster/queue?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Multiple stations should create moderate concentration (festival/mixed flow ~0.30-0.60) but not a single immobile cluster (>0.55-0.85). Choosing min 0.32 helps avoid uniform-random spread (often ~0.10-0.25; random boundary ~0.27). This also excludes STOP's typical ~0.41 only if combined with other metrics; here the band includes 0.41, so we add another metric below to exclude STOP.

Answer submission at stations causes some lingering but most participants still move; real festival viewing is ~0.02-0.36 and standing queues ~0.30-0.60. Using 0.05-0.45 reflects participatory stop-and-go while excluding RANDOM (0.0) and excluding STOP (1.0).

questions.question: T: Is there a clear stop-and-go dynamic (alternating movement and brief stationary periods) rather than steady motion or completely static behavior?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Stop-and-go inflates speed variability compared to homogeneous flow (0.3-0.5). Real mixed transit/festival is ~0.40-0.80; allowing up to 0.9 accommodates stronger intermittency. This excludes STOP (0). RANDOM can still overlap, so we bundle with a discriminating measure below.

Even with stops, travel legs between stations remain purposeful and near-linear; real transit ~0.85-0.97. Setting min 0.8 excludes RANDOM (~0.02) and excludes STOP (0), making the stop-and-go interpretation non-random.

Some agents should be below 0.3 m/s on average due to answering at stations, but not most agents. This range is consistent with festival viewing/participatory pauses and excludes RANDOM (0) and STOP (1).

questions.question: S/R: Do teams tend to converge toward shared station areas (common destinations) rather than dispersing outward from a single start point?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Stations create shared focal endpoints over windows (participants heading toward submission points). Real festival viewing shows convergence ~0.40-0.85; we use a relaxed 0.35-0.8 to avoid overestimation. This excludes RANDOM (typically <0.30) and excludes STOP (0).

The game encourages contraction toward stations rather than radially spreading away; real viewing/festival dispersal_score tends to be negative (about -0.70 to 0.00). Using max 0.1 avoids an 'explicit dispersal' signature (0.30-0.80) and also excludes RANDOM's negative-only tendency only weakly; the bundled convergence_score provides the main discrimination against RANDOM/STOP.

questions.question: R/Safety: Does the crowd avoid physical contact while still exhibiting some close interactions around stations (not zero-contact trivial baselines, not panic pushing)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Station areas and brief crowding can cause occasional close contacts but not panic; real crowded-normal is ~0.001-0.005 and festival/dense viewing ~0.005-0.030. Setting 0.001-0.03 matches participatory station crowding and excludes both RANDOM and STOP (both ~0).
Ensures the scene is not fully halted while collisions occur; also excludes RANDOM high-speed fingerprint (~3.96) and complements collision_fraction which alone could be gamed by near-static jitter.

scenes.description: A small march begins around a banner; demonstrators chant and proceed down the promenade.
scenes.decomposition_reasoning: A demonstrator march implies coordinated forward motion (moderate walking speed), strong common heading (high flow alignment, lower directional entropy), fairly straight paths, and some spatial concentration around a banner without being fully stationary. The description does not mention explicit temporal transitions (e.g., accelerating, dispersing), so trend metrics are avoided. Density/collision are used cautiously: adaptive density overlaps random, and collision_fraction is only informative if we require a nonzero minimum consistent with crowding while staying in the festival/dense-viewing band.

questions.question: V: Do demonstrators move at normal marching/walking speeds (not running, not stopped)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: A march proceeding down a promenade suggests normal urban transit / free walking speeds (0.8–1.5 m/s), not rushing/running. This range excludes RANDOM mean_speed (~3.96–3.99) and excludes STOP (0.0).

A coordinated march should have more homogeneous speeds than a festival/mixed crowd; the homogeneous-flow reference is ~0.3–0.5, so allowing up to 0.6 covers small variations while staying plausible. This band excludes STOP (0.0), and Q1's mean_speed already excludes RANDOM.

questions.question: D: Is the crowd directionally coordinated as a marching stream down the promenade rather than chaotic multi-directional motion?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: A march proceeding together implies festival/event-like streaming toward a shared direction; reference band for event flow is 0.55–0.85 (near-uniform stream up to ~0.95). This lower bound excludes RANDOM flow_alignment (~0.05–0.15) and STOP (0.0).

A march is mostly directional (0.55–0.75 typical for mostly directional; one-way can be ~0.30–0.55). Setting max 0.75 excludes RANDOM (1.0). The min avoids trivially low/degenerate values from near-all-stationary behavior (STOP gives 0.0).

questions.question: R: Are individual trajectories realistically march-like (mostly straight progression with minor deviations), rather than random-walk zigzags?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Marching down a promenade should yield near-straight pedestrian paths; real pedestrian transit is typically 0.85–0.97 (often higher for short tracks). This band strongly excludes RANDOM path_linearity (~0.02) and excludes STOP (0.0).

questions.question: S: Is the crowd spatially concentrated into a stream around the banner rather than uniformly spread across the whole area?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: A march organized around a banner implies a lane/stream and local clustering around the banner, giving festival/mixed-flow concentration; using min 0.35 avoids uniform/random spread (random-walk baseline often ~0.15–0.41, with lower values common). This band helps exclude RANDOM at the low end, while remaining consistent with transit/festival (0.30–0.60).

questions.question: S/R: Does the group exhibit gathering/convergence toward a common moving focal point (the banner) rather than no collective focal behavior?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: March begins around a banner, suggesting people align toward a shared focal region and move together; festival viewing/converging scenes are ~0.40–0.85. Setting min 0.35 excludes RANDOM convergence (~0.09–0.29) and also excludes STOP (0.0).

A march forming around a banner is not described as spreading outward; dispersal_score should be near zero or slightly negative (festival viewing often negative). Capping at 0.05 excludes clear outward dispersal; it also excludes the RANDOM baseline tendency to be negative only weakly (so this metric is mainly to rule out outward-flee dynamics, while convergence_score provides the anti-random signal).

questions.question: T/Activity: Are most agents actively marching rather than lingering/standing still for long periods?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Demonstrators chanting and proceeding implies largely active transit; commuter/transit scenes typically have lingering_fraction 0.00–0.10, while standing audiences/queues are 0.30–0.60. Using max 0.2 allows brief slowdowns near the banner but excludes STOP (1.0). RANDOM is 0.0, so Q6 alone doesn't exclude random; other questions (mean_speed, flow_alignment, path_linearity) handle that.

questions.question: R/Safety: Does the march remain physically plausible with low but nonzero contact consistent with a dense moving group (avoiding both impossible overlaps and trivially zero-contact sparse motion)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: A 219-agent march around a banner suggests crowding where occasional physical-contact events may occur, but not panic/crush; real crowded/festival viewing ranges 0.005–0.030, while crowded-but-normal can be 0.001–0.005. Choosing 0.001–0.03 keeps it realistic while requiring nonzero contact, excluding both RANDOM and STOP (both 0.0).

scenes.description: Smoke from a storage room triggers a fast walk away from mid-promenade, dispersing to remote exits.
scenes.decomposition_reasoning: Scene implies an escape response: fast walking away from a mid-promenade source, with outward dispersal toward multiple remote exits. So questions target (V) elevated speed and possible acceleration, (D) self-organized outward headings with reduced entropy and higher alignment, (S) increased spatial spread and less concentration, (T) clear expanding trends over time (positive dispersal/spread_trend), and (R) realism constraints: high path linearity and low collisions despite density. Metrics are bundled so each question includes at least one band excluding RANDOM (e.g., mean_speed, flow_alignment, directional_entropy, path_linearity, dispersal_score) and at least one excluding STOP (e.g., mean_speed>0, lingering_fraction<0.6, spread_trend>0.1).

questions.question: V: Are agents moving in a fast-walk escape speed regime (not running, not slow viewing)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: “Fast walk away” suggests speeds above normal transit (~0.8–1.3) and below typical running (~1.5–2.5). A 1.1–1.8 band matches brisk/urgent walking and excludes RANDOM baseline (~3.98) and STOP (0).

Escape movement is purposeful but with heterogeneous interactions/avoidance, so CV should be in homogeneous-to-mixed range (~0.3–0.8) rather than panic (0.9+). This band excludes STOP (0) while mean_speed already excludes RANDOM.

questions.question: T/V: Does the crowd show a clear mobilization (accelerating away) rather than constant-speed drifting?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Smoke triggers an escape response, implying increasing motion intensity early on; a positive trend reflects accelerating mobilization. Real-data reference for clear acceleration is ~0.10–0.40; slightly relaxed to 0.08–0.35. This excludes both RANDOM/STOP near 0.

In an escape, lingering should drop as people start moving; real-data mobilizing is -0.40 to -0.10. Using max -0.1 avoids the trivial near-0 trends from RANDOM/STOP and matches a clear decrease in lingering over time.

questions.question: D: Is there a self-organized common flow direction away from the mid-promenade hazard (not chaotic/random headings)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Even with multiple exits, smoke-driven escape creates a coherent away-from-center tendency; expected alignment higher than typical transit (0.30–0.55) but not a perfectly uniform stream (0.80–0.95). This excludes RANDOM (<0.15) and STOP (0).

Escape should reduce heading diversity relative to mixed transit (0.75–0.90) and far below random (≈1.0). Setting max 0.78 targets ‘mostly directional’ (0.55–0.75) with slight allowance for multiple exits while excluding RANDOM.

questions.question: S/T: Do agents disperse outward from the initial mid-promenade region toward remote exits (expanding footprint)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Description explicitly says “dispersing to remote exits,” i.e., radially outward from the initial centroid; real-data explicit dispersal is 0.30–0.80. A slightly relaxed 0.25–0.8 excludes RANDOM (negative) and STOP (0).
Outward dispersal implies increasing mean distance from centroid; real-data expanding is 0.10–0.40. This excludes RANDOM/STOP near 0.

questions.question: S: Does the crowd occupy the promenade more uniformly as they spread to multiple exits (reduced clustering/concentration)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Dispersing to multiple exits should lower concentration toward a single area; values closer to uniform/random-walk (0.10–0.25) than clustered festival (0.35+). Using max 0.35 reflects reduced clustering while excluding STOP’s typical ~0.41 concentration.

Multiple remote exits implies no single shared final centroid; convergence should be at most commuter-like and likely low. Keeping max 0.35 avoids strong gathering (0.60+) and, together with spatial_concentration, rejects STOP (0 is allowed here) while other questions already reject STOP strongly.

questions.question: R: Are trajectories realistically purposeful during escape (mostly straight, not random-walk jagged)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Escape to exits should be goal-directed and near-straight over a camera window; real pedestrian transit is 0.85–0.97. This band strongly excludes RANDOM (~0.02) and STOP (0).

questions.question: R/S: Despite urgency and density, do agents avoid physical contact and keep lingering low (no freezing)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Crowd is large (168) and escaping; some close contacts may occur but not panic/crush. Using crowded-normal to low festival band (0.001–0.03) but capped at 0.02 to avoid panic. Requiring min>0.001 prevents trivial RANDOM/STOP (0) from passing.
Escape implies most agents are moving (not standing); active transit is 0.00–0.10, so max 0.15 is a relaxed bound. This excludes STOP (1.0) while collision_fraction excludes RANDOM (0).

scenes.description: An influencer meet-and-greet is announced; fans hurry toward the pinpointed spot.
scenes.decomposition_reasoning: Scene implies a crowd rapidly moving toward a single focal point (meet-and-greet spot). So we test: (V) high mean speed and some acceleration; (D) strong global alignment and reduced directional entropy; (S) space use becomes more concentrated; (T) clear contracting trend over time; (R) realistic motion should be near-linear, not random; (S/R) crowding increases near the spot (lingering should stay low because they are hurrying). Trend metrics are only used where the description implies build-up over time.

questions.question: V: Are fans moving fast overall (rushing rather than strolling)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: A 'Rushing' scene implies running/fast walking toward the meet-and-greet. Real-data reference for rushing/running is ~1.5–2.5 m/s; we allow slight slack to 2.6. This band excludes the RANDOM baseline (~3.97 m/s) and excludes STOP (0 m/s).

Rushing fans will have mixed pacing (some accelerate, some weave), so CV should be above homogeneous-flow 0.3–0.5 but typically below panic/chaos 0.9+. Using 0.35–0.9 stays within real-data bands (mixed transit/festival 0.4–0.8, chaos 0.9–1.5). This range excludes STOP (0), and the bundled mean_speed already excludes RANDOM.

questions.question: T/V: Is the crowd clearly accelerating as the announcement triggers a rush (not steady-speed motion)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: An announced meet-and-greet suggests a temporal ramp-up: people start hurrying toward the spot, i.e., accelerating. Real-data reference: clearly accelerating 0.10–0.40. This excludes both RANDOM (~0) and STOP (0).
Acceleration should occur within an overall high-speed regime consistent with rushing. Using 1.4–2.6 is aligned with rushing/running references and keeps separation from RANDOM (~3.97) and STOP (0).

questions.question: D: Do agents share a common movement direction toward the pinpointed meet-and-greet spot (organized stream rather than chaotic directions)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: A focal attraction (pinpointed spot) typically yields event-like streaming with strong alignment. Real-data reference for festival/event flow is 0.55–0.85 (near-uniform stream up to 0.95); we allow up to 0.9. This excludes RANDOM (0.05–0.15) and STOP (0).

If most agents head toward one location, velocity directions are less diverse than mixed/random. Real-data: one-way flow 0.30–0.55, mostly directional 0.55–0.75. Setting max 0.75 excludes RANDOM (=1.0). STOP gives 0, but the bundled flow_alignment excludes STOP.

questions.question: R: Are trajectories realistic for purposeful rushing—mostly straight, not random wandering?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Purposeful rushing to a known point should be near-straight over a camera window. Real pedestrian transit is 0.85–0.97; we relax slightly down to 0.82 to allow obstacle avoidance while still far above RANDOM (~0.02) and STOP (0). This strongly excludes both trivial baselines.

Purposeful motion should not look near-uniform random in headings; keeping entropy below 0.85 aligns with mostly directional/mixed-transit upper ranges and excludes RANDOM (=1.0). STOP would be 0 but is excluded by the path_linearity minimum.

questions.question: S/T: Is there clear convergence toward a shared meeting point (many trajectories ending nearer a common centroid)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: A 'pinpointed spot' implies strong convergence. Real-data reference: festival viewing 0.40–0.85; explicit gathering 0.60–0.90. Using 0.45–0.90 fits this and excludes RANDOM (<=~0.29) and STOP (0).

Converging to a focal point corresponds to contraction rather than outward dispersal; dispersal_score should be negative. Real-data: explicit gathering -0.80 to -0.20; festival viewing -0.70 to 0.00. Setting max -0.1 avoids the RANDOM band (about -0.29..-0.08) only partially, so this is bundled with convergence_score which already excludes RANDOM and STOP; together they support contraction-to-point behavior rather than arbitrary motion.

questions.question: T: Does the crowd contract over time as more fans arrive at the meet-and-greet location (not steady spread)?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Announcement-induced rushing implies the group becomes more spatially compact (contracting). Real-data reference: contracting -0.40 to -0.10. Using max -0.1 (with tolerance) excludes RANDOM (~0) and STOP (0).

A focal spot should increase spatial concentration beyond uniform wandering. Real-data: festival/mixed flow 0.30–0.60; explicit single cluster 0.55–0.85. Using 0.35–0.75 captures a noticeable concentration while avoiding the low/uniform random-walk region (random ~0.10–0.25; also anti-reference shows random can reach ~0.41, so we require >=0.35 and rely on the spread_trend to exclude random/stop robustly). STOP is ~0.41 but is excluded by the negative spread_trend requirement.

questions.question: S/R: Does local crowding become meaningfully higher (but not jammed), consistent with fans bunching near the meet spot while still moving?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: A meet-and-greet spot creates a hotspot where some individuals get many close neighbors. Real-data: strong hotspots 4.5–7.0; we set min 5.0 to specifically require a hotspot and reduce overlap with typical scenes and with random clumping (random can be 4.1–6.3, so we push the minimum up). This alone may not fully exclude random, so we bundle with flow_alignment which random fails.

If there is a real hotspot created by purposeful rushing, the overall motion should be aligned toward it (event flow). Requiring flow_alignment >=0.55 matches the event-flow reference and excludes RANDOM (<=0.15) and STOP (0), ensuring the hotspot is not just Poisson clumping.

Because fans are hurrying, most should not be 'lingering' below 0.3 m/s. Real-data: active transit 0.00–0.10; festival viewing can reach up to ~0.36, but this is a rushing scene, so we cap at 0.2. This excludes STOP (=1.0). RANDOM (=0.0) would pass this single metric, but bundled flow_alignment excludes RANDOM.

scenes.description: A vehicle impact shakes a storefront; people flee to the far edges of the open walkway.
scenes.decomposition_reasoning: The scene is a violent vehicle impact causing an urgent outward flight to the walkway edges. This implies (i) high speeds vs normal pedestrian transit, (ii) strong dispersal/expansion away from an initial centroid and toward boundaries, (iii) increased directional organization into a common escape direction (or a few dominant directions) rather than random headings, and (iv) a temporal trend: accelerating early and increasing spread/density changes as people evacuate. To avoid trivial baselines, each question bundles at least one metric that excludes RANDOM (e.g., mean_speed, flow_alignment, directional_entropy, path_linearity) and at least one that excludes STOP (e.g., mean_speed, lingering_fraction). Trend metrics are used only where the description implies change (fleeing/dispersal), with non-zero expected slopes (|trend|>=0.10).

questions.question: V/T: Do people move fast in response to the vehicle impact, with an early acceleration consistent with fleeing?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: A violent impact with people fleeing suggests rushing/running rather than normal transit. Real-data rushing/running is ~1.5–2.5 m/s; allow a slightly relaxed upper bound for variability. This band excludes RANDOM (~3.96) and excludes STOP (0).

Fleeing after an impact implies a clear early acceleration (people start from slower/standing then speed up). Real-data reference for clearly accelerating is 0.10–0.40; this excludes both RANDOM (~0) and STOP (0).

questions.question: R/V: Is there low stationary/lingering behavior (few people remain near-still) despite the chaotic event?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: A panic-like flight implies most agents are moving above 0.3 m/s, so lingering should be low, closer to active transit (0.00–0.10) than viewing/queues. Setting max 0.15 keeps it realistic while excluding STOP (1.00). Note RANDOM is 0, so this measurement alone would not exclude RANDOM; it is used here as a realism/response check rather than a discriminator.
Bundled to ensure discrimination: fleeing implies high mean speed (≥1.3 m/s) consistent with rushing/running (1.5–2.5). This excludes STOP (0) and excludes RANDOM (~3.96) by having a low upper bound.

questions.question: D: Do trajectories become directionally organized into escape flow(s) rather than uniform random headings?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Fleeing toward the far edges implies many people share outward escape directions (one or a few dominant flows), closer to event/evacuation flow (0.55–0.85) than chaotic mixed (0.10–0.30). This excludes RANDOM (0.05–0.15) and excludes STOP (0).

Escape tends to reduce heading diversity versus near-uniform random. A 'mostly directional' to moderately mixed band is ~0.55–0.75; using max 0.8 is relaxed but still excludes RANDOM (1.0). STOP yields 0, but is already excluded by flow_alignment and/or speed in other questions.

questions.question: S/R: Are paths fairly straight (goal-directed) rather than meandering while fleeing to the edges?

measurements.expected_result_reasoning: Fleeing typically produces goal-directed, near-straight paths over the camera window. Real pedestrian transit is 0.85–0.97; set min 0.8 to be tolerant of obstacle avoidance while still far above RANDOM (~0.02) and STOP (0).
Bundled to reinforce 'flight' rather than slow wandering. This range is consistent with fast transit/running and excludes STOP (0) and RANDOM (~3.96 via upper bound).

questions.question: T/S: Does the crowd expand outward over time as people flee from the impact area toward the far edges?
